questions.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={t}^{3}+{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{3}-{t}^{2}$
from $t=0$ to $t=1$ ?
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})=3{t}^{2}+2t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})=3{t}^{2}-2t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{(3{t}^{2}+2t)}^{2}+{(3{t}^{2}-2t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+12{t}^{3}+4{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}-12{t}^{3}+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{18{t}^{4}+8{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\sqrt{18{t}^{2}+8}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-1)=3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)=2t-1.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),\,y=t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ ?
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))^{2}+(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(t)+{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-1,\,y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ ?

To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\cdot 3 \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 2 \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))^{2}+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{36{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)+16{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

$x=t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\,y=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$
from $t=2$ to $t=5$ ?
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))=1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.

$$

$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({cos}^{3}⁡t)=-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{sin}^{4}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{4}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}(-1-1) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(-12\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t)}^{2}+{(12{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{144{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{4}⁡t+144{sin}^{4}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{144{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{144{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}12|\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t|\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}12\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+3\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the arc length $L$ of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=\frac{1}{9}(6t+1)^{3/2},\,y=\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2},\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Do not round the answer.

$L=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{9}(6t+1)^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot \frac{3}{2}(6t+1)^{1/2}\cdot 6 \\  & =(6t+1)^{1/2},\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}) \\  & =3t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{((6t+1)^{1/2})}^{2}+(3t)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{6t+1+9{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{(3t+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}|3t+1|\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2}+t)\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{3}{2}+1)-0 \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010979/assets/ac040bc2c3eb943f947f34602c7c03e90f18e129a0fa7749d8ae60faaab12f71.png)

Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\pi ].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

According to the double-angle formula for cosine, $\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .$ Substituting $\theta =\frac{t}{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{t}{2}) & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}) \\ 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}) \\ 2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =4{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\text{d}t \\  & =-2\cdot 2\cdot {\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2})|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-4(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-4(0-1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010979/assets/834eff403ac2a6f696e104ec914cac1b951f8a6d989e11c0e9f2576ac9e7f0d8.png)

Find an integral expression for the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=1-t, \quad y= \dfrac{2}{3} t^{3/2}, \qquad t\in[0,1].
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\:\textrm{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2})={t}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{(-1)}^{2}+{({t}^{1/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the expression that gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=t, \, y=\ln{(\cos{t})}$
from $t=0$ to $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (see graph below).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010979/assets/48de26c11ae08afb45ec19ee56e770f7418f9be2afb8ee7dd46a0d1136cb125b.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\:\textrm{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡t))=-\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{tan}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+{tan}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=e^t(\cos{t}+\sin{t}), \quad y=e^t(\cos{t}-\sin{t}) , \quad t\in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right].
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010979/assets/15d185178bf8882f837c19361d630c0e537e145ca2337cad4655677255d0348a.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)) \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)) \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{4{e}^{2t}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{e}^{t}{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =2({e}^{\pi /4}-1).\end{aligned}
$$
